questions.stem_text:
A1. This question is about power output of an outboard motor.
A small boat is powered by an outboard motor of variable power P. The graph below shows the
variation with speed v of P when the boat is carrying different loads.
P / kW
v / ms−1
The masses shown are the total mass of the boat plus passengers.

questions.stem_text:
A1. Data analysis question
At high pressures, a real gas does not behave as an ideal gas. For a certain range of pressures,
it is suggested that the relation between the pressure P and volume V of one mole of the gas at
constant temperature is given by the equation
PV = A + BP
where A and B are constants.
In an experiment to measure the deviation of nitrogen gas from ideal gas behaviour, 1 mole
of nitrogen gas was compressed at a constant temperature of 150 K. The volume V of the gas
was measured for different values of the pressure P. A graph of the product PV of pressure
and volume was plotted against the pressure P and is shown below. (Error bars showing the
uncertainties in measurements are not shown).

P / ×106Pa

A1. The question is about investigating a fireball caused by an explosion.

form of a circular fireball. Knowing the speed with which these fireballs can spread is of
great importance to fire-fighters. In order to be able to predict this speed, a series of controlled

questions.stem_text:
A1. This question is about electrical resistance of the metal mercury.
The resistance R of a sample of mercury was measured as a function of the temperature T of
the sample. The sample was cooled and data points were taken at temperature intervals
of 0.2 K. The uncertainties in R and T are too small to be shown on the graph.
[figure]
The hypothesis is that resistance is proportional to absolute temperature for temperatures
greater than 4.5 K.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: (a) (i) Suggest whether the data supports the hypothesis.
parts.markscheme_text: no the graph is not linear / not a straight line; [1]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: This question invited the students to make simple common sense deductions from a rather unusual graph. In such cases the students need to spend time understanding the situation. This involves careful reading. Most students overlooked the statement that the uncertainties were „too small to be shown on the graph‟. Hence they tried to stitch together the two parts of the graph with one smooth line instead of going through each and every point shown. A (a) displayed many misconceptions and inaccurate use of language. It should be noted that the word proportional only refers to a straight line passing through the origin. Other ways of describing a relationship are: „linear‟, „non-linear’ (giving a curve) and ‘exponential’. These words have very specific meanings and students need to know how to use them accurately. The students who had accurately understood the situation being graphed were able to answer

questions.stem_text:
A1. Data analysis question.
Metal girders are often used in buildings that have been constructed to withstand earthquakes.
To aid the design of these buildings, experiments are undertaken to measure how the natural
frequency f of horizontal oscillations of metal girders varies with their dimensions. In an
experiment, f was measured for vertically supported girders of the same cross-sectional area
but with different heights h.

h
ground surface

parts.text: (a) Draw a best-fit line for the data.
parts.markscheme_text: f / Hz 70 60 50 40 30 20 10 0 0 5 10 15 20 25 h / m smooth curve as above; (judge by eye) [1] Do not allow point-to-point curve. Do not allow curve to "curl round" at low or high h. Single "non-hairy" line only is acceptable.
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (a) Candidates were required to draw a smooth curve through a series of points. Few could do this adequately and it was rare to see a good construction. Lines were usually point-to- point, kinked in some way, or “hairy” (meaning that the candidate had a number of separate attempts to draw the line). This is evidently not a skill that all candidates possess. There is still a widespread misconception that when the question asks for the candidate to “draw a best-fit line” this implies that the line is straight. This error is seen in work representing all the IB languages and is a simple point that traps candidates year after year.

questions.stem_text:
A1. Data analysis question.
The movement of glaciers can be modelled by applying a load to a sample of ice.
ice sample
change in height
height
load
ice sample
After the load has been applied, it is observed to move downwards at a constant speed v as
the ice deforms. The constant speed v is measured for different loads. The graph shows the
variation of v with load W for a number of identical samples of ice.
The data points are plotted below.
[figure]
Error bars for v are shown for two data points. The uncertainty in W is negligible.

parts.text: (a) On the graph opposite, draw the line of best-fit for the data points.

questions.stem_text:
A1. Data analysis question.
A capacitor is a device that can be used to store electric charge.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: (i) On the graph opposite, draw a best-fit line for the data starting from t = 0.
parts.lead_in: (a) An experiment was undertaken to investigate one of the circuit properties of a capacitor. A capacitor C was connected via a switch S to a resistance R and a voltmeter V. S C R V The initial potential difference across C was 12 V. The switch S was closed and the potential difference V across R was measured at various times t. The data collected, along with error bars, are shown plotted below. [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: smooth curve; that passes through all error bars; 15 10 V / V 5 0 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 t / s [2]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (a) (i) Few candidates scored full marks. Too often examiners saw poor quality draughtsmanship and ruler-straight lines through the first three points. Most candidates were able to ensure that their lines stayed within the bounds of the error bars. Candidates are encouraged to read through the whole question before attempting to answer – had this been done then they might have gained additional clues from what followed. It should be noted that the skill being tested here was the ability of the candidates to ignore the points and draw a smooth curve through the uncertainty bars.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) It was hypothesized that the decay of the potential difference across the capacitor is exponential. Determine, using the graph, whether this hypothesis is true or not.
parts.lead_in: (a) An experiment was undertaken to investigate one of the circuit properties of a capacitor. A capacitor C was connected via a switch S to a resistance R and a voltmeter V. S C R V The initial potential difference across C was 12 V. The switch S was closed and the potential difference V across R was measured at various times t. The data collected, along with error bars, are shown plotted below. [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: correctly identifies three points from own graph; correctly processes these three points using exponential/half life/constant ratio/ relationship; to conclude that decay is exponential; within uncertainty; [4]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (ii) Good tests of exponential change were beyond many. Examiners expect to see a systematic test carried through accurately. A suitable test might include identification of half- life behaviour, constant ratio behaviour, or fitting to an exponential function. Each of these approaches could have scored full marks. Often there were vague and meaningless statements about the asymptotic behaviour of the graph.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: (i) initial rate of decay of potential difference V.
parts.lead_in: (b) The time constant τ of the circuit is defined as the time it would take for the capacitor to discharge were it to keep discharging at its initial rate. Use the graph in (a) to calculate the
parts.markscheme_text: evaluates a gradient over a minimum of 5 s to give an initial ⎫ ⎛ 12 ⎞ -1 ⎪⎬ (allow ECF rate for example, ⎜ = ⎟ 1.3 V s for graph above; from the graph) ⎝ 9.5 ⎠ ⎪⎭ V s⁻¹ ; Clear evidence of calculation of gradient must be seen. [2]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (b) (i) This was adequately done by about half of the candidates although there were few confident tangents seen by examiners. Errors were to omit the unit and to try to work out a gradient over the full 30s.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) time constant τ.
parts.lead_in: (b) The time constant τ of the circuit is defined as the time it would take for the capacitor to discharge were it to keep discharging at its initial rate. Use the graph in (a) to calculate the
parts.markscheme_text: obtains evidenced answer for t intercept; [1]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (ii) Examiners expected to see an evidenced solution. Candidates who wrote down the answer without explanation gained little credit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) The time constant τ = RC where R is the resistance and C is a property called capacitance. The effective resistance in the circuit is 10 MΩ. Calculate the capacitance C.
parts.markscheme_text: C = ⎛ ⎜ 10 = ⎞ ⎟ 1.0 ( ± 0.2) × 10 -6 Ω -1 s/F ; ⎝ 10 × 10 6 ⎠ Award [0] for absence of 106 unless unit is in terms of MΩ. [1]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (c) The answer here had to use the answer to (b)(ii) and most candidates were able to do this satisfactorily. A substantial number failed to take account of the prefix to the unit in the resistance and were a factor of 106 out in their answer.

questions.stem_text:
A1. Data analysis question.
A particular semiconductor device generates an emf, which varies with light intensity.
The diagram shows the experimental arrangement which a student used to investigate the
variation with distance d of the emf ε . The power output of the lamp was constant. (The power
supply for the lamp is not shown.)
mV
semiconductor
device
lamp
d
The table shows how ε varied with d.
[figure]

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Outline why the student has recorded the ε values to different numbers of significant digits but the same number of decimal places.
parts.markscheme_text: reference to meter/instrument; reference to constant accuracy/precision; [2]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (a) Many candidates failed to recognise that the number of decimal places is a reflection of the precision of a piece of equipment – it this case the millivoltmeter. Using different number of significant figures simply indicates that the reading is larger or smaller but it will be to the same precision. A sizeable proportion of candidates believed the number of decimal places was something that they could choose in an arbitrary manner.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: (i) Explain why this procedure can be used to disprove the student's suggestion but it cannot prove it.
parts.lead_in: (b) On looking at the results the student suggests that ε could be inversely proportional to d. He proceeds to multiply each d value by the corresponding value of ε .
parts.markscheme_text: looking for constant value; clear deviation means not/unlikely to be valid; close to constant only means possibility of validity; [2 max]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment:
(i) Most candidates were able to correctly plot the data point despite there being a relatively difficult scale division.

(i) Most candidates failed to realise that the result of multiplying a series of corresponding values of ε and d only needed to show different values for the equation to be disproved but that all possible values would need to be taken prove it (clearly an impossibility).

in (i) most candidates showed that there was too large a discrepancy between the three sets of products to suggest that the equation was viable.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) Using the data for d values of 19.1 cm, 16.0 cm and 10.0 cm discuss whether or not ε is inversely proportional to d.
parts.lead_in: (b) On looking at the results the student suggests that ε could be inversely proportional to d. He proceeds to multiply each d value by the corresponding value of ε .

questions.stem_text:
1.
Data analysis question.
An array of photovoltaic cells is used to provide electrical energy for a house. When the
array produces more power than is consumed in the house, the excess power is fed back into
the mains electrical supply for use by other consumers.
The graph shows how the power P produced by the array varies with the time of day.
The error bars show the uncertainty in the power supplied. The uncertainty in the time is
too small to be shown.
[figure]
06:00
07:00
08:00
09:00
10:00
11:00
12:00
time of day / hour

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Using the graph, estimate the time of day at which the array begins to generate energy.
parts.markscheme_text: smooth curve drawn through all error bars and curve extrapolated appropriately to x-axis; their own intercept correctly read to within ± 6 minutes (1 small square) / 7:50 hour to 8:00 hour if no line drawn; [2]
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: (a) Most candidates understood the requirements of the question. They were able to draw an acceptably smooth curve extrapolated to the time axis. There were fewer poor quality lines than in previous examinations. Nevertheless, a substantial minority ended the curve at a time of 08:30 and then quoted this time as that at which the solar panels began to generate energy. Some drew a straight line (that could not possibly touch all the error bars) and extrapolated this line to a time of about 07:30. Some credit was available for this.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: (b) The average power consumed in the house between 08:00 and 12:00 is 2.0 kW. Determine the energy supplied by the array to the mains electrical supply between 08:00 and 12:00.

parts.examiner_comment: (b) This was poorly done from two points of view. It was clear that there was widespread misunderstanding of the relationship between energy and power units. Many candidates could get no further forward than calculating the energy used by the house in the four-hour time period. Most were unable to recognise that the energy supplied to the grid was related to the area under the graph.

Award [3] for a bald correct answer. Award [2 max] if gradient is left as a fraction. [3]

questions.stem_text:
1.
Data analysis question.
An experiment is undertaken to investigate the relationship between the temperature of a ball
and the height of its first bounce.
A ball is placed in a beaker of water until the ball and the water are at the same temperature.
The ball is released from a height of 1.00 m above a bench. The maximum vertical height h
from the bottom of the ball above the bench is measured for the first bounce. This procedure
is repeated twice and an average hmean is calculated from the three measurements.
1.00 m
point of release of the ball
maximum vertical position of the ball
h
bench
The procedure is repeated for a range of temperatures. The graph shows the variation
of hmean with temperature T.
[figure]

In an investigation a student folds paper into cylinders of the same diameter D but different
heights. Beginning with the shortest cylinder they applied the same fixed load to each of the
cylinders one by one. They recorded the height H of the first cylinder to collapse.
H
D

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Suggest why the student's data supports the theoretical prediction.
parts.markscheme_text: theory H = cD^(2/3) predicts that H³ ∝ D² ✓ graph of H³ vs D² is a straight line through the origin / graph of proportionality ✓ Allow H = cD ( ) ( ) 2 3 gives H3 = c3D2 for MP1. Do not award MP2 for "the graph is linear" without mention of origin. 2
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment:
Load on a cylinder. The question was successful for candidates well prepared to write conclusions in their lab reports. Theory in the stem of the question predicts a directly proportional relationship between H and

D2/3, which graphed are H3and D2. Well prepared candidates were able to identify, that the theory predicts that H3should be directly proportional to D2 and that this proportionality can be seen from the graph. Many candidates were able to mention that the relationship was linear and passed through the origin (as an alternative to proportional). However, a common response mentioned only linear or linear regression which is not sufficient to fully demonstrate proportionality. Part b) was the most difficult part of section A, but still accessible. Many candidates only calculated the slope of the graph and did not realise that the third root of the slope is the constant c. Some students who were able to achieve the numerical value of c=1.4 struggled to establish the correct unit - perhaps lacking confidence or familiarity with the notion that a unit could be raised to a fractional index. In c) most of the candidates well identified the load or the type of the paper as possible controlled variables. A common mistake here was answer discussing the height or the diameter of the cylinders.

parts.markscheme_text: theory H = cD^(2/3) predicts that H³ ∝ D² ✓ graph of H³ vs D² is a straight line through the origin / graph of proportionality ✓ Allow H = cD ( ) ( ) 2 3 gives H3 = c3D2 for MP1. Do not award MP2 for "the graph is linear" without mention of origin. 2
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment:
Load on a cylinder. The question was successful for candidates well prepared to write conclusions in their lab reports. Theory in the stem of the question predicts a directly proportional relationship between H and

D2/3, which graphed are H3and D2. Well prepared candidates were able to identify, that the theory predicts that H3should be directly proportional to D2 and that this proportionality can be seen from the graph. Many candidates were able to mention that the relationship was linear and passed through the origin (as an alternative to proportional). However, a common response mentioned only linear or linear regression which is not sufficient to fully demonstrate proportionality. Part b) was the most difficult part of section A, but still accessible. Many candidates only calculated the slope of the graph and did not realise that the third root of the slope is the constant c. Some students who were able to achieve the numerical value of c=1.4 struggled to establish the correct unit - perhaps lacking confidence or familiarity with the notion that a unit could be raised to a fractional index. In c) most of the candidates well identified the load or the type of the paper as possible controlled variables. A common mistake here was answer discussing the height or the diameter of the cylinders.

A student conducts an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal cube.
The cube is heated in a beaker of boiling water to a temperature of 100 °C and then quickly
transferred into an insulated vessel of negligible thermal capacity. The vessel contains water
at 20 °C and of known specific heat capacity.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) State one other measurement that the student will need to make.
parts.markscheme_text: final temperature of equilibrium/water/cube OR mass of water/cube ✓ Do not award mark if any additional incorrect measurement is included Accept temperature change if water or cube specified 1
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: Most answers referred to measuring the mass of the cube or the mass of the water in the vessel. There were some strange references to time, room temperature and the specific heat of water, but in general this was a high-scoring question, reaching 90% in HL.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: (b) Suggest one modification that the student can make to reduce the fractional uncertainty for the change in temperature of the metal cube.
parts.markscheme_text: smaller mass of cube OR hotter cube OR more mass of water OR colder water OR more precise thermometer ✓ Accept reference to repeating the experiment and taking mean values. parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: Answers which increased the temperature change of the cube were marked correct. Several students scored, with references to higher initial temperature of the cube (no need to explain how) or through colder water, or by changing consistently the mass of the cube or the water used. However, many students gave answers such as 'use more water or a colder cube’ which have exactly the opposite effect. Some students gave answers which improved the overall reliability of the experiment but did not reduce the uncertainty in the cube's change of temperature.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) Some water from the beaker is accidentally transferred with the cube. Discuss how this will affect the value of the calculated specific heat capacity of the cube.
parts.markscheme_text: cube specific heat will be too large/increased value/overestimate ✓ additional «thermal» energy transferred OR temperature rise of water will be larger OR temperature drop of cube will be smaller ✓ 2 Section B
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: Adding boiling water with the cube will decrease the temperature change of the cube and increase the apparent specific heat capacity. There was a split between excellent justified answers and several students who said exactly the opposite. There were also too many vague answers such as 'the temperature change will increase' without specifically identifying which change they were referring to.

aluminium block

parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.

parts.examiner_comment: Travelling wave. The question is based on a simple method of measuring the speed of sound in the air. Most of the data are provided in the form of a graph. Two identical small spheres, each of mass m, are placed at equal distances from the centre

different values of the distance of separation of the spheres d, in metres.

parts.text: (a) (i) Explain why m was kept constant.
parts.markscheme_text: identifies m as a controlled variable OR recognizes that «the variation of» m affects T OR identifies d as the independent variable OR relationship between d and T could not be found if m changes OR acknowledges that only one variable is to be changed at a time OR highlights the need of the same conditions throughout the experiment ✓ OWTTE. 1

parts.examiner_comment: Even from high scoring students answers to this question were disappointing. Mass m is kept constant as it is a controlled variable and would alter the time period if changed. A typical wrong answer was that m must be constant so that the rod is balanced.

1.
A student performs an experiment with a rod that is free to oscillate in a horizontal plane.
Two identical small spheres, each of mass m, are placed at equal distances from the centre
of the rod. The student records values of the period of oscillation of the rod T in seconds for
different values of the distance of separation of the spheres d, in metres.
[figure]
The student plots the variation with d of T, keeping m constant.
00
T / s
d / m

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: (a) (i) Explain why m was kept constant.
parts.markscheme_text: identifies m as a controlled variable OR recognizes that «the variation of» m affects T OR identifies d as the independent variable OR relationship between d and T could not be found if m changes OR acknowledges that only one variable is to be changed at a time OR highlights the need of the same conditions throughout the experiment ✓ OWTTE. 1
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: High scoring students did not have an issue with this initial question, although there were far too many who did not articulate correctly. Mass m is kept constant as it is a controlled variable and would alter the time period if changed. Any of these two reasons scored. A typical wrong answer was that m must be constant so that the rod is balanced.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) The student proposes the hypothesis that T is directly proportional to d. Outline whether the graph supports this model.
parts.markscheme_text: no, as the fit does not go through the origin ✓ 1
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: More than half the students easily scored here, although there are still far too many students who think a straight line implies that a proportional relationship exists even when it does not pass through the origin.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: (iii) State one other feature of the experiment that the student should keep constant.
parts.markscheme_text: amplitude/angle of release / use of small angle OR number of oscillations OR any measurable feature of the cable, e.g. length or diameter OR any measurable feature of the rod OR cable holding the rod at its mid-point OR shape of masses ✓ Do not accept same cable/rod/ spheres without any other reference. Do not accept any environmental reference as e.g. temperature. 1
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: Many students showed a lack of awareness of experimental technique. The natural answer was that the angle of release should be kept small or constant but the range of answers was surprising. Perhaps the word feature in the stem led students to pick irrelevant answers which ended up accepted in the markscheme (MS). Answers seen included tension in the cable, temperature of the room, distance between the masses or keeping windows closed. Variables that can actually be measured were accepted unless related to the environment, such as temperature, pressure windows closed. Distance between masses was not accepted as it constitutes the independent variable manipulated.

parts.markscheme_text: correct shape of graph ✓ intercept on T axis is not zero ✓ 2

parts.examiner_comment: Straight lines or increasing parabolas were more popular than the relationship required. A reasonable number of correct answers were seen.

parts.markscheme_text: Read their R₀ from the y-intersection ✓ α = gradient/R₀ OR substitute into equation coordinates of a point on the line ✓ Correct calculation of their alpha ✓ K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹ ✓ If line not drawn or extended to y-axis, accept R₀ from 5.6 to 6.1. Allow ECF for MP3.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Determine g using the photograph.
parts.markscheme_text: Read at least two points correctly and consistently ✓ Use with a length interval from two non-consecutive points OR for two (or more) length intervals, using consistent time intervals ✓ Correct calculation of g ✓ Award [2] max if they use one single length interval of consecutive points. Award [1] max if they miss to subtract the initial point in their length interval or if they use inconsistent time intervals. Do not penalize significant figures in the final answer. 3
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: A range of strategies were observed and accounted for in the MS. The question discriminated well, showing best students choosing the simplest strategy of selecting the longest interval and obtaining g = 9.75 (ms-2) using 19.5 cm and 0.2 s in the equation. The range of strategies allowed for points to be read at either (5.0, 6.2, 9.8, 15.9 and 24.5) cm with a tolerance of 0.1 cm or their corresponding values considering top or bottom of the circle. Students who chose any interval with non-consecutive points were allowed to obtain full marks. Students who used an interval of two consecutive points were penalized once, and those who succeeded to use the equation and reading data but omitted the subtraction of the initial position were given only one mark, as the students who messed up and did not use a consistent time for the length of the interval chosen. The average was over 2 marks showing a solid ability to face this calculation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: (b) The percentage uncertainty in t is ± 5 %. Estimate the absolute uncertainty in your value of g.
parts.markscheme_text: Use 10% for delta t2 ✓ Estimate an uncertainty for s using an absolute of 0.5 OR 1 mm AND propagate it to 1/their length interval OR 2/their length interval respectively ✓ Add both relative or percentage uncertainties AND calculate the absolute uncertainty ✓ Allow ECF for MP3. Do not penalize significant figures in the final answer. 3
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: This question was less successful than a). An easy mark was for propagating the time uncertainty correctly using 10%. Another for a correct determination of the uncertainty in distance and finally an ECF mark for the absolute uncertainty. Several complete and correct answers were seen although all kinds of errors were present, from using 5% to ignoring the uncertainty in distance to expressing the percentage without calculating the absolute uncertainty. The average was close to 1.5 marks which shows an acceptable performance of students.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) Suggest a suitable value for the maximum duration of the flash.
parts.markscheme_text: Flash must be so short that blurring is within the absolute uncertainty / error of determination of s ✓ (Final) speed is around 2 m s⁻¹ and error is about 1 mm so (maximum) duration around 1 2000 s ✓ Award [1] max if they argue that images might merge and state a maximum of 0.025 s (or less). Award [1] max if they use the uncertainty of time and state a time of (2 x) 0.05 x 0.05 s = 0.005 s (or less). Award MP2 if they state an interval of 0.001 s or less. 2
parts.usable_if: Syllabus fit has not been reviewed. The earlier question is included as provisional practice; check the original question and marking conventions.
parts.examiner_comment: A challenging final question. As it was clear from the standardization that very few were relating the duration of the flash to the velocity of the ball to minimize the blurring and therefore the uncertainty in the position, alternative answers as applying the 5% uncertainty of the time to the multi-flash intervals or estimating a value smaller than half that value as not to merge the images were given partial recognition. It was evident during marking that most students did not interpret the question properly.

questions.stem_text:
1.
A student is analysing a sample of water. To determine its density, the student measures
the volume with a measuring cylinder and the mass with an electronic balance.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Identify one way to ensure that the volume is read accurately. The following data are collected: Volume = (10.6 ± 0.2) cm³ Mass = (10.82 ± 0.01) g
parts.markscheme_text: Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus OR placed on a horizontal surface so that the cylinder is vertical OR eyes levelled with the reading ✓ Do not award vague statements such as "horizontal reading" or repeat measurements or improving precision or parallax error without a way to improve it [1]
parts.examiner_comment: This was answered correctly by most students. A common incorrect answer was to repeat the measurements to create an average. This response does not answer the question as given which was how to make the single measurement more accurate.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: (b) (i) Calculate the density of the sample and its absolute uncertainty.
parts.markscheme_text: ρ = <<10.82/10.6>> = 1.02 ✓ Δρ/ρ = 0.2/10.6 + 0.01/10.82 = 0.0198 so Δρ = 0.02 ✓ Award MP2 if they use the fractional uncertainty in volume only AND state that the fractional / absolute uncertainty in mass can be neglected. Allow 1020 kg m-3 and ∆p=20 DO NOT penalize for SF. [2]
parts.examiner_comment: Most students were able to calculate density with only a small minority using the values as written (volume above the mass) instead of substitution into the correct equation. Most students were able to propagate the uncertainty using the percent uncertainties while a small number of students solely added the absolute uncertainties. There was ECF allowed from bi) to bii) but this proved difficult for some students who may have forgotten to convert the uncertainty as well. This question asked for the correct precision in the final answer. The uncertainty should only have 1 significant figure. There may be exceptions to this in an internal assessment, but students should be directed to using only one SF on exams. In addition, the value of the density cannot have a precision greater than the precision indicated by the uncertainty (1021±20 is not acceptable).

parts.text: (ii) State your answers in kg m-3 and with correct precision. When the density was measured, the sample was at 35 °C. The student has a graph that shows the variation with temperature of the density of pure water. [figure] density of pure water / kg m−3 temperature / °C
parts.markscheme_text: ρ = ± 1020 20 ✓ Watch for ECF from bi) For ECF, density must be in kgm-3 AND correct corresponding uncertainty. The density should have 3SF, and corresponding precision in the uncertainty. [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Most students were able to calculate density with only a small minority using the values as written (volume above the mass) instead of substitution into the correct equation. Most students were able to propagate the uncertainty using the percent uncertainties while a small number of students solely added the absolute uncertainties. There was ECF allowed from bi) to bii) but this proved difficult for some students who may have forgotten to convert the uncertainty as well. This question asked for the correct precision in the final answer. The uncertainty should only have 1 significant figure. There may be exceptions to this in an internal assessment, but students should be directed to using only one SF on exams. In addition, the value of the density cannot have a precision greater than the precision indicated by the uncertainty (1021±20 is not acceptable).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) Suggest whether the water sample can be considered pure.
parts.markscheme_text: reads 994 (±1) «kg m-3» at T = 35°C ✓ value outside the range «1020±20»so sample is not pure ✓ Watch for ECF from bii) Allow 1020±20 does not include the value of a pure sample at 35°C so it is not pure for MP2 [2]
parts.examiner_comment: A large proportion of the responses seem to assume that the graph presented was experimental data and did not read that the graph represented the real data for pure water. Many incorrect answers expected water to either always have a constant value of 1000 kgm-3 or that it should have decreased linearly with temperature. This is also an example to teach the students in test taking skills. Part a) and b) both required uncertainties in their answer and this should be considered when answering part c). Too many students did not get full marks as the range of possible values was not included in their explanation.

2.
A group of students is investigating refraction in a semi-circular glass block.
Light from a ray box enters the curved side of the block. The light passes through the block
and leaves, refracted, at P.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) Outline how the students can ensure that the light is not deflected at the curved surface. The students vary the position of the ray box to obtain data to determine the refractive index of the glass. They use a protractor to collect values for the angles of incidence θi and refraction θr at P and record them on a table. semi-circular glass block air P ray box
parts.markscheme_text: measure P to be at the centre of the flat edge/side so that incident rays are aimed at P /go through radial lines OR check that the incident angle is 0° at every point of incidence ✓ [1]
parts.examiner_comment: These parts of the question were fairly well done in both HL and SL on a common experiment. Most students realised that all angles should be measured from the normal and referred to this in their answers.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: (b) (i) One of their measurements is shown. State θr for this measurement. [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: θ = 49 r ✓ Accept correct answer only [1]

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) Complete the table. θi θr sin θi sin θr [figure] They plot a graph of the variation with the sine of θi of the sine of θr . They add uncertainty bars for sin θr for the first and last data point and draw the best-fit line. sinθr sinθi [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: 0.755 ✓ Accept only 0.755. Answer must be quoted to 3 sf. [1]

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: (c) (i) Determine the gradient of the students' best-fit line.
parts.markscheme_text: use two points from the line that use more than half the line of best fit ✓ gradient = 1.5 ✓ Allow (implicit) use of the origin. Look for ∆x ≥ 0.3 [2]
parts.examiner_comment: Students showed a good knowledge of calculating gradients. There were many points on the graph that they could easily read for the calculation. Some students chose data points from the table and not from the line of best fit. It should be noted that in general, data points should not be used to calculate the gradient as only points from line of best fit should be used.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) Draw on the students' graph the line of maximum gradient.
parts.markscheme_text: draw max from lower end of lower error bar to upper end of upper error bar ✓ [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Students were asked to draw a maximum line of best fit. It was easy to draw this so that the line was contained with in all of the error bars. This is the preferred method rather than just using the error bars of the first and last points. Surprisingly some students left this blank while others drew a parallel line above the given line of best fit. Max/min lines of best fit should be known to all students as part of the Internal Assessment and these skills may also be assessed in paper one b.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: (iii) Determine the value of the refractive index of the glass with its absolute uncertainty.
parts.markscheme_text: States gradient gives the value of the refractive index OR n=1.5 ✓ n=1.5±0.2 ✓ MP1 can be shown as an equation Candidates may calculate the uncertainty by using the gradient of the line found in cii) or finding the average of the max and min lines of best fit. Look for working leading to 0.1≤ ∆n ≤ 0.2 [2]
parts.examiner_comment: This question expected a lot of work for just 2 marks. For the first mark, the students needed to recognise that the gradient gave the refractive index of the glass. Thus, to determine the uncertainty of the refractive index, they needed to get the uncertainty of the gradient. This is not the same as using the uncertainty of the data points. If this was an internal assessment, it would be expected that the students would draw a maximum and minimum line of best fit. Then they would calculate the uncertainty of the gradient using (max-min)/2. For only 1 mark, it was decided that just using the gradient from the maximum line drawn in 2cii) and using only its deviation was acceptable. It should be noted that this is not best practice and would not be the proper method on an internal assessment. Students also needed to show how the uncertainty was determined, and it was not sufficient to only write a value.

parts.markscheme_text: Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus OR placed on a horizontal surface so that the cylinder is vertical OR eyes levelled with the reading ✓ Do not award vague statements such as "horizontal reading" or repeat measurements or improving precision or parallax error without a way to improve it [1]

parts.examiner_comment: Most students were able to calculate density with only a small minority using the values as written (volume above the mass) instead of substitution into the correct equation. Most students were able to propagate the uncertainty using the percent uncertainties while a small number of students solely added the absolute uncertainties. There was ECF allowed from bi) to bii) but this proved difficult for some students who may have forgotten to convert the uncertainty as well. This question asked for the correct precision in the final answer. The uncertainty should only have 1 significant figure. There may be exceptions to this in an internal assessment, but students should be directed to using only one SF on exams. In addition, the value of the density cannot have a precision greater than the precision indicated by the uncertainty (1021±20 is not acceptable).

Most students were able to propagate the uncertainty using the percent uncertainties while a small number of students solely added the absolute uncertainties. parts.label: (c)(i)

parts.markscheme_text: use two points from the line that use more than half the line of best fit ✓ gradient = 1.5 ✓ Allow (implicit) use of the origin. Look for ∆x ≥ 0.3 [2]

Some students chose data points from the table and not from the line of best fit. It should be noted that in general, data points should not be used to calculate the gradient as only points from line of best fit should be used.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: (ii) Draw on the students' graph the line of maximum gradient.
parts.markscheme_text: draw max from lower end of lower error bar to upper end of upper error bar ✓ [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Students were asked to draw a maximum line of best fit. It was easy to draw this so that the line was contained with in all of the error bars. This is the preferred method rather than just using the error bars of the first and last points. Surprisingly some students left this blank while others drew a parallel line above the given line of best fit. parts.examiner_comment: This question expected a lot of work for just 2 marks. For the first mark, the students needed to recognise that the gradient gave the refractive index of the glass. Thus, to determine the uncertainty of the refractive index, they needed to get the uncertainty of the gradient. This is not the same as using the uncertainty of the data points. If this was an internal assessment, it would be expected that the students would draw a maximum and minimum line of best fit. Then they would calculate the uncertainty of the gradient using (max-min)/2. For only 1 mark, it was decided that just using the gradient from the maximum line drawn in 2cii) and using only its deviation was acceptable. It should be noted that this is not best practice and would not be the proper method on an internal assessment. Students also needed to show how the uncertainty was determined, and it was not sufficient to only write a value.

parts.examiner_comment: Most students were able to provide a good reason why collecting only one data value is not a good method. questions.stem_text:
1.
A group of students is trying to determine the density and the viscosity of a liquid.
To determine the density, they use a balance to read the mass m of a sphere in air and
immersed in the liquid.
They use a sphere of volume V = 1.827 × 10⁻⁷ m³.
The readings are mair = 1.427 g in air and mlmmersed = 1.208 g in the liquid.
The readings are different due to buoyancy. The buoyancy force Fb is given by
Fb = ρ V g,
where V is the volume of the sphere and ρ is the density of the liquid.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) State the level of precision in the measurement of m.
parts.markscheme_text: milligram OR 0.001 g ✓ Accept half milligram / 0.0005 g Ignore use of plus/minus [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Many student question required an exact figure. In addition, other common incorrect responses referred to accuracy, decimal places, or had the incorrect power of ten (e.g. 0.1g).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: (b) Show that Fb is about 2 mN.
parts.markscheme_text: OR 2.1 mN ✓ Allow the calculation to give a result in mN or N. Look for full substitution or answer with at least two SF. [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Students needed to calculate the difference in weight in air and in the liquid. Few students got this question right. Many of the students attempted to use the equation and the density calculated from 1c. This method could not be accepted as it required the value, 2mN, that needs to be shown thus no marks could be awarded for this method.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) Calculate the density of the liquid. To determine the viscosity, they immerse the sphere in the liquid and drop it from rest. They collect values and plot a graph of the position d of the sphere from the moment they drop it. They verify that the sphere reaches terminal velocity vt after 0.5 s. [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: ✓ = 1200 kg m-3 ✓ Do not penalise the use of SF. Watch for ECF from 1b and POT errors. [2]
parts.examiner_comment: Many students received full marks even if they could not complete 1b. A common error was to forget to convert the buoyant force from mN to N.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: (d) Draw the line of best fit on the graph.
parts.markscheme_text: A single, straight line passing through most points, which does not attempt to pass through the origin. ✓ Curved line passing through first three points ✓ Allow MP1 straight lines to extend to the x-axis [2]
parts.examiner_comment: This graph represents two different motions that has been clearly indicated in the question. This means that the line of best fit also has two expected sections. One section is a curved line at the beginning while the sphere is accelerating and then a straight line while it is at terminal velocity. Many students tried to create a single fit line. Forcing it through the first and last point missed too many points and scored zero. It is important to note that the first and last points on a graph are no more important than any other point and lines of best fit should be created taking into consideration all points. Poor drawings included ones

parts.text: (e) Outline how the students may verify that the sphere reaches terminal velocity. They repeat the experiment several times and estimate an average for vt = (0.71 ± 0.05) m s⁻¹. They use the equation η = m g V g rv air t 6 , where r = radius of the sphere, vt = terminal velocity of the sphere, η = viscosity of the liquid. The radius r of the sphere is 3.520 mm.

parts.examiner_comment: The question required the students to outline how to verify the sphere is a terminal velocity. Students were not awarded a mark for solely describing or defining terminal velocity as this is does not verify if the sphere reaches terminal velocity. To achieve the mark, students, needed to explain how use the experimental data to determine terminal velocity was reached which required a reference to the graph.

parts.label: (f)
parts.text: (f) Calculate the viscosity of the liquid and its absolute uncertainty. Ignore uncertainties in the mass, radius and volume of the sphere. Give your answer in the form η ± Δη, to an appropriate number of significant figures, including units. The students search literature values and find the viscosity of this liquid to be 0.24, when expressed in SI base units.
parts.markscheme_text: = 0.2512 ✓ 7% OR 0.02 ✓ = 0.25 0.02 ✓ Pa s OR kg m-1 s⁻¹ ✓ MP1 and MP2 are for the calculations, accept any number of SF, MP3 is for the matching precision of the value and its uncertainty. ECF may apply but uncertainty may only have 1SF. Allow other suitable units such as Nm-2s [4]
parts.examiner_comment: There were few students that received full marks for this question. Many students received the first mark point for the substituting the values into the given equation, though POT errors were frequent. Some students were able to get the second mark point for calculating the percent uncertainty although many incorrectly wrote this as an absolute uncertainty. The third mark point was for matching the precision of the absolute uncertainty and the calculated value of the viscosity. It is important to remind teachers and students that uncertainties should only have 1 significant figure. The value of the viscosity should be rounded to the same precision. It was unfortunate to see many students did not include a unit for the fourth mark point even though the question clearly asked for an appropriate unit.

parts.examiner_comment: Many student but this did not receive a mark. Since the command term used is suggest, students need to provide a reason for the conclusion. Part f) asked the students to calculate an experimental answer including an uncertainty and this should be considered and commented on when looking at the value given in part g).

parts.examiner_comment: Very few students received full marks on this question. From there, they could compare the gradient of the experimental data and the equation to show the relationship. questions.stem_text:
1.
A group of students is trying to determine the density and the viscosity of a liquid.
To determine the density, they use a balance to read the mass m of a sphere in air and
immersed in the liquid.
They use a sphere of volume V = 1.827 × 10⁻⁷ m³.
The readings are mair = 1.427 g in air and mlmmersed = 1.208 g in the liquid.
The readings are different due to buoyancy. The buoyancy force Fb is given by
Fb = ρ V g,
where V is the volume of the sphere and ρ is the density of the liquid.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: (a) State the level of precision in the measurement of m.
parts.markscheme_text: milligram OR 0.001 g ✓ Accept half milligram / 0.0005 g Ignore use of plus/minus [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Many student question required an exact figure. In addition, other common incorrect responses referred to accuracy, decimal places, or had the incorrect power of ten (e.g. 0.1g).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: (b) Show that Fb is about 2 mN.
parts.markscheme_text: OR 2.1 mN ✓ Allow the calculation to give a result in mN or N. Look for full substitution or answer with at least two SF. [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Students needed to calculate the difference in weight in air and in the liquid. Few students got this question right. Many of the students attempted to use the equation and the density calculated from 1c. This method could not be accepted as it required the value, 2mN, that needs to be shown thus no marks could be awarded for this method.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: (c) Calculate the density of the liquid. To determine the viscosity, they immerse the sphere in the liquid and drop it from rest. They collect values and plot a graph of the position d of the sphere from the moment they drop it. They verify that the sphere reaches terminal velocity vt after 0.5 s. [figure]
parts.markscheme_text: ✓ = 1200 kg m-3 ✓ Do not penalise the use of SF. Watch for ECF from 1b and POT errors. [2]
parts.examiner_comment: Many students received full marks even if they could not complete 1b. A common error was to forget to convert the buoyant force from mN to N.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: (d) Draw the line of best fit on the graph.
parts.markscheme_text: A single, straight line passing through most points, which does not attempt to pass through the origin. ✓ Curved line passing through first three points ✓ Allow MP1 straight lines to extend to the x-axis [2]
parts.examiner_comment: This graph represents two different motions that has been clearly indicated in the question. This means that the line of best fit also has two expected sections. One section is a curved line at the beginning while the sphere is accelerating and then a straight line while it is at terminal velocity. Many students tried to create a single fit line. Forcing it through the first and last point missed too many points and scored zero. It is important to note that the first and last points on a graph are no more important than any other point and lines of best fit should be created taking into consideration all points. Poor drawings included ones

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: (e) Outline how the students may verify that the sphere reaches terminal velocity. They repeat the experiment several times and estimate an average for vt = (0.71 ± 0.05) m s⁻¹. They use the equation η = m g V g rv air t 6 , where r = radius of the sphere, vt = terminal velocity of the sphere, η = viscosity of the liquid. The radius r of the sphere is 3.520 mm.
parts.markscheme_text: The gradient is constant / the line is straight « when terminal v is reached » ✓ Ignore any comments not explicitly referring to the graph [1]
parts.examiner_comment: The question required the students to outline how to verify the sphere is a terminal velocity. Students were not awarded a mark for solely describing or defining terminal velocity as this is does not verify if the sphere reaches terminal velocity. To achieve the mark, students, needed to explain how use the experimental data to determine terminal velocity was reached which required a reference to the graph.

parts.label: (f)
parts.text: (f) Calculate the viscosity of the liquid and its absolute uncertainty. Ignore uncertainties in the mass, radius and volume of the sphere. Give your answer in the form η ± Δη, to an appropriate number of significant figures, including units. The students search literature values and find the viscosity of this liquid to be 0.24, when expressed in SI base units.
parts.markscheme_text: = 0.2512 ✓ 7% OR 0.02 ✓ = 0.25 0.02 ✓ Pa s OR kg m-1 s⁻¹ ✓ MP1 and MP2 are for the calculations, accept any number of SF, MP3 is for the matching precision of the value and its uncertainty. ECF may apply but uncertainty may only have 1SF. Allow other suitable units such as Nm-2s [4]
parts.examiner_comment: There were few students that received full marks for this question. Many students received the first mark point for the substituting the values into the given equation, though POT errors were frequent. Some students were able to get the second mark point for calculating the percent uncertainty although many incorrectly wrote this as an absolute uncertainty. The third mark point was for matching the precision of the absolute uncertainty and the calculated value of the viscosity. It is important to remind teachers and students that uncertainties should only have 1 significant figure. The value of the viscosity should be rounded to the same precision. It was unfortunate to see many students did not include a unit for the fourth mark point even though the question clearly asked for an appropriate unit.

parts.label: (g)
parts.text: (g) Suggest a conclusion reached by the students.
parts.markscheme_text: the value lies within the range of the uncertainties <<so the experiment was accurate>> ✓ Watch for ECF from 1f [1]
parts.examiner_comment: Many student but this did not receive a mark. Since the command term used is suggest, students need to provide a reason for the conclusion. Part f) asked the students to calculate an experimental answer including an uncertainty and this should be considered and commented on when looking at the value given in part g).

parts.examiner_comment: This was well done by most students which required students to make straight forward calculations and round to the appropriate number of decimal places. parts.markscheme_text: manipulates SB law using logs ✓ relates 4 from SB to 3.99 in the equation of line of best fit as the same ✓ [2]
parts.examiner_comment: Very few students received full marks on this question. Students needed to manipulate the Stephan- Boltzmann law using logarithms so that it was laid out in a similar fashion as the line of best fit. From there, they could compare the gradient of the experimental data and the equation to show the relationship. It should be noted that the command term explain does not imply that only words are expected. The manipulation of equations is a form of communicating ideas and relating theory to experimental data. Just stating the gradient was calculated by log (L/R2)/log(T) (from the axes labels) was not enough to relate this to the Stephan-Boltzmann law.
